title: Practice and joy
goal: Recognise 学 (learn) and 习 (practise), and understand the idea of returning to learning.
intro: Confucius asks about the pleasure of returning to what we learn; start with 学 (learn) and 习 (practise).

aids.text: Isn’t it a pleasure to learn and keep practising what you have learned?

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted draft)
rights.note: AI-assisted learner wording pending human review. The external link is comparison material only; no verified attribution to, or adaptation of, the linked translator is claimed.

aids.text: The question invites us to share the pleasure of learning. Zhu Xi’s discussions include returning to a passage and thinking it through again as forms of practice; this is more than repeating sounds. The rest of Analects 1.1 turns to friendship and remaining untroubled when others do not recognise us.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: Zhu Xi, Zhuzi yulei, compiled by Li Jingde, vol. 20, 學而時習之章; CText links the Siku Quanshu edition
rights.note: Independent English summary of an ancient discussion; no CText AI/crowdsourced English translation is reproduced. Link for comparison only.

aids.text: 学习之后，常常练习，会让人感到快乐。

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted draft)
rights.edition: Wuhua teaching paraphrase of the pinned source excerpt
rights.note: Existing Chinese teaching paraphrase checked against its source excerpt; retained as a separate draft layer. This is Wuhua wording, not a quotation from a historical commentator.

aids.text: 学 (xué) means “learn”; 习 (xí) means “practise”, and 之 points back to what was learned. Here 说 is read yuè and means “pleasure”, rather than shuō, “speak”.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: Analects 1.1; James Legge, The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861)
rights.note: New learner explanation; pinyin remains separately aligned and unreviewed.

exercises.feedback: 学 means “learn”. You met it at the start of the line. 习 (xí) is “practise”. Return to the words whenever you need help.

exercises.prompt: Which action fits the idea in this passage?
options: Return to practise what you learned
exercises.feedback: The line links learning with returning to practise. The final question presents that practice as a pleasure. 说 is read yuè here, meaning pleasure, not shuō (“speak”).

reflection: What is one small thing you would like to practise again? You may answer in English or simply think about it.

title: A teacher beside you
goal: Recognise 人 (person) and 师 (teacher), and notice how learning can begin with the people around us.
intro: Who can we learn from? Look for 人 (person) and 师 (teacher) in this line about walking with others.

aids.text: Walking with others, I am sure to find someone I can learn from.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted draft)
rights.note: AI-assisted learner wording pending human review. The external link is comparison material only; no verified attribution to, or adaptation of, the linked translator is claimed.

aids.text: 人 (rén) means “person”, and 师 (shī) means “teacher”; 我师 means “my teacher”. 三人行 pictures three people walking together: 三 is “three”, and 行 is read xíng, “walk”, here.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: James Legge, The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861); Project Gutenberg eBook 3330, Book VII (Shu R), chapter XXI
rights.note: Independently written learner material; historical source linked for comparison. Modern website adaptations are not reproduced. Content and teaching review pending.

aids.text: The next part of the same passage explains how to learn from others: follow what is good, and use their mistakes to examine and correct oneself. Calling someone a teacher here need not give them a formal title. The emphasis is on noticing opportunities to learn, not copying everything a person does.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: James Legge, The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (1861); Project Gutenberg eBook 3330, Book VII (Shu R), chapter XXI
rights.note: Independently written learner material; historical source linked for comparison. Modern website adaptations are not reproduced. Content and teaching review pending.

exercises.prompt: Which character means “teacher” in this line?
exercises.feedback: 师 means “teacher”. 人 means “person”, and 行 is “walk” in this sentence; 我师 means “my teacher”.

exercises.prompt: Which action follows the wider passage’s idea of learning from others?
options: Learn from good qualities and reflect on mistakes
Only learn from people with a formal title
exercises.feedback: The following sentence makes a distinction: follow good qualities and use mistakes as a reason to examine oneself. Learning from someone is not the same as copying everything they do.

reflection: Think of someone you learned from outside a classroom. What did you notice, and how did it change what you do? You may answer in English.

title: Knowing others, knowing yourself
goal: Recognise 知 (know) and 自 (self), and notice a contrast in a classical line.
intro: This line turns from knowing other people to knowing ourselves; look for 知 (know) and 自 (self).

aids.text: To understand other people is to be wise; to understand yourself is to see clearly.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted draft)
rights.note: AI-assisted learner wording pending human review. The external link is comparison material only; no verified attribution to, or adaptation of, the linked translator is claimed.

aids.text: Chapter 33 compares understanding others with understanding ourselves, then makes a similar comparison between overcoming others and overcoming ourselves. Reading the paired phrases together draws attention inward. Here “clarity” is a way of describing self-understanding, rather than a score or a claim that someone knows everything.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: James Legge, The Tao Te Ching (1891), chapter 33
rights.note: Independently written learner material; historical source linked for comparison. Modern website adaptations are not reproduced. Content and teaching review pending.

aids.text: 了解别人是一种智慧，了解自己会让人更清醒。

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted draft)
rights.edition: Wuhua teaching paraphrase of the pinned source excerpt
rights.note: Existing Chinese teaching paraphrase checked against its source excerpt; retained as a separate draft layer. This is Wuhua wording, not a quotation from a historical commentator.

aids.text: 知 (zhī) means “know” or “understand”; 人 (rén) means “person”, while 自 (zì) turns the phrase toward oneself. 者 (zhě) points to the person who does this, and 明 (míng) suggests clarity here.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: James Legge, The Tao Te Ching (1891), chapter 33
rights.note: Independently written learner material; historical source linked for comparison. Modern website adaptations are not reproduced. Content and teaching review pending.

exercises.prompt: Which character means “know” in this line?
exercises.feedback: 知 means “know”. 人 means “person”; 自知 directs knowing back toward oneself.
知人 points to knowing other people. 自知 points to knowing yourself. English translations such as “wisdom” and “clarity” help us notice the contrast without claiming there is only one interpretation.

reflection: Think of something you understand about another person, and something you are still learning about yourself. You may write a thought or a question in English.

title: What counts as enough?
goal: Recognise 足 (enough) and 富 (rich), and explore a different meaning of being rich.
intro: What makes someone rich? Explore how 知足 (knowing enough) changes the meaning of 富 (rich).

aids.text: A person who knows when they have enough is rich.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted draft)
rights.note: AI-assisted learner wording pending human review. The external link is comparison material only; no verified attribution to, or adaptation of, the linked translator is claimed.

aids.text: 足 (zú) means “enough” here, and 知足 (zhī zú) means being content with enough. 富 (fù) means “rich”; 足 can also mean “foot”, but that is not its meaning in this phrase.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: James Legge, The Tao Te Ching (1891), chapter 33
rights.note: Independently written learner material; historical source linked for comparison. Modern website adaptations are not reproduced. Content and teaching review pending.

aids.text: The same chapter has just compared knowing others with knowing oneself. This short claim presents contentment as a kind of richness; it does not count possessions or say that everyone already has what they need. For this lesson, we notice how the meaning of 富 changes when it is paired with 知足.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: James Legge, The Tao Te Ching (1891), chapter 33
rights.note: Independently written learner material; historical source linked for comparison. Modern website adaptations are not reproduced. Content and teaching review pending.

exercises.prompt: In 知足 (zhī zú), what does 足 mean?
exercises.feedback: Here 足 means “enough”. Together, 知足 describes recognising enough and feeling content; the everyday meaning “foot” does not fit this phrase.

exercises.prompt: What does this line connect with being rich?
exercises.feedback: The line connects 富, “rich”, with 知足, knowing enough. It invites us to consider contentment as a kind of richness, rather than a comparison of possessions.

reflection: Think of one moment when something felt sufficient. What made it feel like enough? English is welcome; this is a personal reflection.

title: A different view of “I”
goal: Recognise 我 (I/me) and 与 (with), and connect the line to its questioning context.
intro: Zhuangzi brings 我 (I/me) together with all things; follow 与 (with), then explore why the passage keeps questioning this claim.

refs.label: Zhuangzi · Discussion on Making All Things Equal

aids.text: Heaven and earth come into being with me, and all things form one with me.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted draft)
rights.note: AI-assisted learner wording pending human review. The external link is comparison material only; no verified attribution to, or adaptation of, the linked translator is claimed.

aids.text: The surrounding passage unsettles familiar comparisons of size and length of life. After joining “me” with all things, it asks what happens when we put “one” into words: does naming it create another distinction? This learner explanation follows that turn in the argument, rather than treating the short quotation as its final answer.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: James Legge, The Writings of Chuang Tzu (1891), book II, The Adjustment of Controversies

aids.text: 从这个角度看，我与天地万物并不是截然分开的。

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted draft)
rights.edition: Wuhua teaching paraphrase of the pinned source excerpt
rights.note: Existing Chinese teaching paraphrase checked against its source excerpt; retained as a separate draft layer. This is Wuhua wording, not a quotation from a historical commentator.

aids.text: 我 (wǒ) means “I” or “me”, and 与 (yǔ) means “with”; 万物 (wàn wù) means all the many things in the world. 为 (wéi) is read wéi here in 为一, “form one”, rather than wèi, “for”.

rights.author: Wuhua (AI-assisted editorial explanation)
rights.edition: James Legge, The Writings of Chuang Tzu (1891), book II, The Adjustment of Controversies
rights.note: Independently written learner material; historical source linked for comparison. Modern website adaptations are not reproduced. Content and teaching review pending.

exercises.prompt: Match 与 (yǔ) in this line with its English meaning.
exercises.feedback: 与 links two sides: 天地与我 (heaven and earth with me). 我 means “I” or “me”, according to its role in an English sentence.

exercises.prompt: How does the surrounding passage affect our reading?
options: It continues questioning even the claim of “one”
It gives a modern scientific measurement
exercises.feedback: After asserting “one”, the text questions what happens when we say it. Returning to context keeps a memorable quotation from becoming an oversimplified final answer.

reflection: Look back at 我 (I/me) and 与 (with). What question does the line raise for you about your relationship with the world? English is welcome; there is no single required answer.
